\title{Shortfall of Domestic Resources to Eradicate Extreme Poverty by 2030:\\ An Update with the September 2026 PIP Data}
\author{Adrien Fabre\thanks{CNRS, CIRED. E-mail: adrien.fabre@cnrs.fr.}}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
I update \cite{fabre_shortfall_2025} with the September 2026 release of the World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP), which expresses incomes in 2021 PPPs and includes more recent surveys for 118 of the 168 countries covered. The method is unchanged. When the original \$2.15 line is converted to 2021 prices (\$2.46), the results are very close to the original ones: with a balanced growth of 3\% per year between 2022 and 2030, \upRatePovThreeEq\% of humans would still live in extreme poverty in 2030 (vs. \PaperRatePovThree\%), and even capping incomes at \$7.84 a day cannot eradicate extreme poverty in \upNbCapEq{} low-income countries (vs. 5). At the new international poverty line of \$3.00 a day, which is higher in real terms, the shortfall is more severe: \upRatePovThree\% of humans would remain extremely poor, and \upNbCapEight{} low-income countries could not eradicate extreme poverty even by capping incomes at \$8.30 a day. Even by 2035, \upNbCapTF{} low-income countries would lack the resources to end extreme poverty at \$3.00 a day. In contrast, a transfer of \upGapThree\% of global income would suffice to close the global extreme poverty gap in 2030.
\end{abstract}
